description: Soy Denis Javier Garcia Cortez, Ingeniero Agroindustrial y de Biocomercio, especialista en investigación y análisis de datos. Lidero MUYUY INNOVA, un equipo que impulsa soluciones científicas y tecnológicas. Busco programadores, ingenieros, investigadores, especialistas en IA, datos, agricultura sostenible, diseñadores y comunicadores. Valoramos la creatividad, el compromiso y el trabajo colaborativo para transformar desafíos globales en soluciones innovadoras.
summary: Muyuy is a decision-support tool that helps smallholder farmers on Peru's coast, in the Andes and in the Amazon explore what to rotate over their next three seasons. On a phone, even offline, the farmer picks their farm on the map, answers what they know, and sees their options in Spanish, English or Quechua. Muyuy tests up to 2,744 rotations of 31 crops and intercrops against 45 years of daily NASA POWER climate (1981 to November 2026), corrected to the farm's elevation with SRTM and combined with SoilGrids soil data. Each rotation is scored with transparent models: FAO-56 water balance, nitrogen, pests, carbon, RUSLE erosion, frost, hail and excess rain. The result is not "the best rotation" but three options with their robustness ("works 6 years out of 10"), compared with what the farmer grows today, with the reasons, evidence, risks and data gaps for each. Muyuy also says when to plant, shows the El Niño forecast and tests every rotation against the 2041-2060 climate. Young farmers in Chulucanas, Piura, have already tested it in the field. Muyuy never replaces the farmer's judgment: it shows what the data say, and the farmer decides.

Live app: https://muyuy-innova.onrender.com

Code and architecture: https://github.com/patente012026/muyuy

Complete technical document: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1c6tZS74QduESmwaEu8bIFEj1sPjIPzCG

What does it do and how does it work?

Muyuy is a decision-support tool that helps smallholder farmers in Peru's coast, Andes and Amazon explore crop rotations for their next three seasons. The farmer picks their farm on a map (or finds it by community name), answers what they know (previous crop, priorities such as saving water, extra income, fodder or better soil, and limits such as frost, hail or terraces), and Muyuy compares at least three rotations, including the one they grow today.

Behind it, a Python engine tests up to 2,744 rotations of 31 crops and intercrops against 45 years of daily NASA POWER climate (1981 to November 11, 2026), downscaled to each farm with SRTM elevation and slope and combined with SoilGrids soil data. Rainfall is cross-checked with ERA5. Each rotation is scored with transparent, standard models: FAO-56 daily water balance, FAO-66 yield response, nitrogen balance, organic carbon, pest-cycle breaks, RUSLE erosion, and frost, hail and excess-rain risk. Historical patterns use Theil-Sen trends, Mann-Kendall tests, El Niño year classes (NOAA ONI) and clustering. Every rotation is also tested against the 2041-2060 climate (median of five NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 models, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5).

For each option Muyuy shows its robustness ("works 6 years out of 10"), why it was suggested, the evidence behind it, its benefits for soil and water, where data are missing, and which risks need local review. It then gives a season plan from planting to sale, the El Niño forecast, and a chat that answers questions with the farm's own data. A technical view for extension workers adds MODIS greenness (2001-2026), live NASA GIBS layers (SMAP soil moisture, GPM IMERG rainfall, GEDI aboveground biomass) and a recent 30 m image of the farm from HLS (Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2). All of Peru is precomputed in 398 NASA POWER cells; online, any place in the world can be computed, with 12 example farms in Africa, Asia and Latin America. All data were downloaded and recalculated on November 14-15, 2026.

What benefits does it have?

- Works offline on any phone as an installable web app: no app store and no good connection needed.

- Reaches farmers where they already are: a WhatsApp/Telegram bot that understands voice notes, and a one-page printed calendar.

- Speaks Spanish, English and Quechua, with voice at every step.

- Transparent: every number traces back to an equation, every crop parameter carries its source and confidence level, and limits are shown, not hidden.

- Zero running cost for the farmer.

What is the intended impact?

To help families reduce losses from frost, drought and El Niño, and to choose rotations that rebuild soil nitrogen and organic matter, cut erosion and save water, while keeping income. Muyuy supports decisions; it does not make them. Each card asks "Would you try it on your farm?" and a "Before you decide" note reminds the farmer that the choice is theirs. Young farmers in Chulucanas, Piura, have already tested Muyuy on their own phones in the field; the next step is a pilot with one community and a review of the Quechua by a native speaker.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

Python (pandas, FastAPI, fpdf2) for data, engine, API and printed PDFs; HTML and JavaScript for the offline web app (PWA); Jupyter notebooks and automated tests for validation; faster-whisper for voice transcription; Claude for understanding farmer messages; Supabase with free Groq and Z.ai models for the chat; Piper and Meta MMS-TTS for app voices; Render for hosting; Blender and ElevenLabs for the video. No special hardware: it runs on an ordinary smartphone.

How is your project creative?

It builds on Andean rotation knowledge, the "muyuy" and the "laymi", instead of replacing it. The conversation starts from the years the community remembers (such as strong El Niño years), risk is drawn as ten squares instead of percentages, and a communal muyuy game lets village assemblies learn with their own history. Instead of naming one "best rotation", it measures how robust each option is across 45 real climate years and the future climate.

What factors did your team consider?

- Low literacy and limited technical experience: icons, voice, "out of 10" risk, short sentences.

- Poor connectivity and cheap phones: offline mode, small downloads, WhatsApp and paper.

- Language: Quechua support, marked as a draft until a native speaker reviews it.

- Data uncertainty: NASA POWER is coarser than ground stations, so rainfall is cross-checked with ERA5 and compared with SENAMHI stations; calibration with PISCO and CHIRPS is planned, and low-confidence crop values are flagged for agronomist review.

- Three very different regions: separate crop tables for highlands, northern coast and upper rainforest.

- Privacy: no names or phone numbers are sent to AI models, and chat questions are not stored.

- Responsible AI: AI only listens and talks; rotations are computed by a transparent engine, and the farmer decides.
